ETL vs. ELT: What's the Difference?
Two letters apart, but they change how your data pipeline runs.
ETL vs. ELT: What's the Difference?
ETL and ELT are the two main ways to move data from one system to another. The difference is small on paper and significant in practice: WHEN the data gets transformed.

E, T and L stand for Extract, Transform and Load — and the middle letter is the whole debate. In ETL, data is Extracted, Transformed (cleaned and reshaped), then Loaded. In ELT, data is Extracted and Loaded first, and Transformation happens later inside the target system.

ETL processes data in a separate engine before it reaches the target. It suits traditional databases and cases where the target is not powerful enough to transform at scale, or where you need strict quality checks before anything arrives.

ELT loads raw data into a modern cloud warehouse or lake, then transforms it with the target's own computing power. It is faster to move, keeps the raw source data available, and lets analysts re-shape it as new questions arise.

There is no universal winner. Choose ETL when transformation quality must be guaranteed before loading and when the target is a conventional database. Choose ELT when you use a scalable warehouse or lake, when source volumes are large, and when you want the flexibility to define new transformations without re-loading.

We review your sources, targets and reporting needs, then design pipelines that use the right pattern per workload — often a sensible mix. We build with scheduling, monitoring and documentation so the pipeline keeps running after we leave.

When 'by tomorrow morning' is too late.

For decades, business reporting ran on nightly batches — data moved overnight and teams saw yesterday's world. Today many decisions benefit from fresher information. Here is how real-time integration works and when it is actually worth it.

For a manufacturer, a dashboard that reflects inventory ten minutes ago beats one from last night. For a logistics firm, shipment events feed customer updates automatically. The value of real-time data grows the closer the decision sits to the event.

Batch moves data in scheduled chunks and is perfectly fine for many needs — simple, cheap and reliable. Real-time integration moves changes as they happen using two main techniques: Change Data Capture (CDC), which watches database logs, and event streaming, which carries messages through platforms like Apache Kafka.

CDC reads the database's transaction log and publishes changes as events; streaming platforms store and deliver those events to subscribers such as analytics tools, caches or other systems. Consumers can replay the event history if they fall behind, which makes this approach far more reliable than point-to-point scripts.

Start honest: which decisions genuinely improve with fresher data? Start with one high-value feed — say, orders feeding a live dashboard — prove the pattern, then expand. Real time is an option, not a mandate.

We help you decide where real-time integration pays off, then design and build the CDC or streaming pipeline with proper ordering, monitoring and failover — connected cleanly to your existing batch architecture.

The quiet fix behind dependable business data.

Your company probably has the same customer in five places — spelled five different ways. Master data management (MDM) is the discipline that brings order to information like this, and it is easier to understand than the acronym suggests.
An MDM program in plain steps

Master data is the core information your business depends on to operate: customers, suppliers, products, employees and locations. Unlike transaction records (an invoice, a shipment), master data changes slowly but is referenced by almost everything else. When a customer's master record is wrong, every invoice, order and report that uses it inherits that error.

The goal of MDM is a 'golden record' — one best version of each entity assembled from all the partial versions scattered across your systems. With matching logic, duplicates are detected and merged, conflicts are resolved by agreed rules, and one trustworthy record is published back to the systems that need it.

Master data becomes messy for predictable reasons: different systems hold different fields, teams enter data without common standards, acquisitions add new systems, and no single owner guards the definitions. The result is duplicated mailings, misquoted prices and dashboard numbers that never quite agree.
An MDM program in plain steps

A practical MDM effort usually looks like this: (1) inventory where master data lives, (2) choose a starting entity — often customers — (3) agree on definitions and rules, (4) build matching and merge logic, (5) assign stewardship so humans resolve the edge cases, and (6) monitor quality over time. It does not need to start with expensive software; process and ownership often deliver the first wins.

We help you scope an MDM program that fits your size, starting with the entity that causes the most pain. We handle the assessment, design the golden-record rules, and help you stand up stewardship — then hand it over with documentation your team can maintain.

Bad data is not an IT problem — it is a business problem.

Every decision your business makes runs on data: forecasts, inventory, pricing, hiring. When that data is quietly wrong, problems surface as lost revenue and frustrated customers — never as 'a data-quality incident.'

Data quality is how well your data serves its purpose. It is commonly described with six dimensions: accuracy (is it correct?), completeness (is anything missing?), consistency (does it agree across systems?), uniqueness (any duplicates?), timeliness (is it current?) and validity (does it obey the rules?).

Bad data shows up in uninviting ways: duplicate mailings and wasted ad spend; quotes built on stale prices; inventory that does not match reality; and leadership teams arguing over which dashboard is right. Fixing the underlying data is usually far cheaper than living with the consequences.

Improvement starts with profiling — measuring how bad things actually are against those six dimensions. Then you fix the specific problems found, standardize how data enters systems, and add monitoring so quality does not quietly decay again.

Begin with the datasets your biggest decisions depend on, not all your data at once. Measure today's state, fix the worst offenders, and assign an owner for each key dataset. A small, sustained program beats a large one-off cleanup every time.
We run a data-quality health check, show you the exact issues and their business impact, then help you fix root causes and set up the monitoring and ownership that keep quality high.

At the outset of every engagement, a Quality Plan tailored to client requirements is developed. It defines data quality metrics, architectural templates, and checkpoints across every stage, from requirements gathering through post-go-live support.

At engagement close, the full team holds a lessons-learned review covering resources, data governance, adherence to standards, customer satisfaction, and quality metrics. Leadership identifies improvements for future engagements.

How does CDC differ from batch ETL?
ETL moves data on a schedule in batches. CDC captures changes as they happen at the source and moves only those changes, giving near-real-time results with far less load.
Does CDC only work with specific databases?
It is most common with major relational databases (such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle) and works with managed cloud databases as well.
Will CDC slow our production database?
Log-based CDC reads the database's own change logs, which is designed for this purpose and typical impact is minimal compared with full dumps.

What is the difference between ETL and ELT?

Both move data between systems. ETL transforms the data before loading it into the target; ELT loads the raw data first and transforms it inside the target warehouse. ELT suits large cloud warehouses; ETL suits traditional databases and complex transformations at the source.

Kafka is a popular open-source platform for streaming events. It reliably stores and delivers messages at massive scale, making it a common backbone for real-time integration.
Is streaming always better than batch?
No. Batch is simpler and perfectly adequate for many reporting needs. Streaming earns its place where recency matters — we help you decide honestly.
What happens if a consumer goes down?
Events are retained on the stream, so the consumer can resume from where it stopped — one of the main reliability benefits.

It is the single, best version of a piece of master data — for example one customer record — assembled from all the partial versions stored across your systems.
Is MDM the same as a data warehouse?
No. A warehouse stores data for reporting. MDM keeps your core business entities (customers, products, vendors) accurate and consistent at the source, feeding the warehouse and everything else.
Do we need new software for MDM?
Often not. We first look at what you already own. Many MDM projects reuse existing databases and tools with a well-designed matching and stewardship process.
